query: A TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy has been reported in a single-phase BCC, dendritic state, with a yield strength of about 800 MPa and roughly 40% strain under lower-temperature testing, but at 1273 K it retains only 330 MPa yield strength and 423 MPa compressive strength at 30% strain. For its use as an intermediate layer that transfers heat between W and CuCrZr while preserving structural integrity, what single intervention could overcome this loss of strength at elevated temperature? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the reported baseline, define the applicable thermal and mechanical boundary conditions, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thermomechanical treatment, such as hot isostatic pressing, to the TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy will enhance its yield strength and compressive strength at elevated temperatures by refining the grain size and stabilizing the BCC phase.
generation.structural_mediator: grain size refinement and BCC phase stabilization
generation.mechanism: thermomechanical treatment-induced grain refinement and phase stabilization
generation.predicted_outcome: 20% increase in yield strength and 15% increase in compressive strength
generation.baseline: 330 MPa yield strength and 423 MPa compressive strength at 30% strain
generation.uncertainty: The actual increase in strength may vary depending on the specific processing conditions and material composition.

falsification_experiment.design: controlled experiment with untreated and hot isostatic pressed TiVNbTa samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the yield strength and compressive strength of the treated sample are not significantly higher than those of the untreated sample, the hypothesis is falsified, with a threshold of 5% increase in strength

cited_evidence.text: Fig. 3a shows the tensile stress–strain curves of ht-TiVNb. The alloy has moderate strength at RT, with a yield strength of ∼647 MPa, a tensile strength of 680 MPa and an elongation of 15 %, i.e. it has no advantages over typical medium- and high-entropy alloys. However, its strength does not significantly decrease at medium and high temperatures, remaining at 405 MPa at 800 °C. This indicates the advantage of a weak dependence of strength on temperature. Fig. 4 shows the fracture surface of ht-TiVNb after tension. Shear plastic deformation and cavity-aggregated dimples appear after applying tension at RT. Tensile fracture at 600 °C is characterised by plastic deformation near the grain boundaries and trans-granular quasi-cleavage within the grains, accompanied by oxidation. Fracture at 800 °C shows an intergranular fracturing mode with notable high-density slip lines and traces of tearing, indicating strong intragranular bonding forces. The fracture surface is covered with an oxide layer, indicating that the alloy is susceptible to oxygen-induced intergranular embrittlement at this temperature. The rapidly advancing aerospace industry has a significant demand for high-performance, high-temperature-resistant superalloys. Ni-based superalloys are extensively employed in hot-section aero-engine components due to their outstanding high-temperature properties, including high strength, fatigue resistance, and creep resistance [,,]. However, the practical application temperature of most nickel-based superalloys is limited to approximately 1150–1200 °C [,,]. Therefore, exploring high-performance superalloys within alternative alloy systems, such as Nb-based [] and Co-based [], is significant. Senkov [,] was the first to apply the high-entropy alloy concept to develop a series of refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). The NbMoTaW RHEAs, fabricated via arc melting, not only retain a stable single-phase BCC structure at 1400 °C but also exhibit a compressive yield strength of 405 MPa, compressive strength of 600 MPa, and compressive strain of 27% under compression at 1600 °C. Although their high-temperature mechanical properties significantly exceed nickel-based superalloys, their compressive strain at room temperature is limited to only 1.5%.
